title: The commute
hook: travel time can be practice time

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Compline, the monks' night prayer that gives the day a clear edge. Your line was done for today.

A train car in the morning, rows of heads bent over glowing screens. A line of cars at a red light. A bus window streaked with rain. Between the start of the workday and its end there's a stretch that belongs to neither home nor work, and it's easy to treat it as time to be killed. Henry David Thoreau, in his essay Walking, says he has met hardly anyone who understood the art of walking, who had, as he puts it, a genius for sauntering. Then he tells a story about where that word came from. Today: the commute.
screen: `HEADS BENT OVER SCREENS.` → `TIME TO BE KILLED?` → `A GENIUS FOR SAUNTERING.`

segments.voice: First, Thoreau's story. He says saunter comes from idlers in the Middle Ages who roamed the country asking for charity on the pretense of going to the Holy Land, à la Sainte Terre, until children cried, there goes a Sainte-Terrer, a saunterer, a Holy-Lander. Whether or not a dictionary agrees, his point is clear: a walk can be a small pilgrimage. Second, a psalm for the trip. In the King James Bible, Psalm 121 ends: "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore." The whole commute fits in one line. Third, a prayer for the road. Jewish tradition has Tefilat HaDerech, the traveler's prayer, said when setting out on a journey, asking to be brought to the destination in peace and returned in peace. The road itself is a place where something deserves to be said. Fourth, the steps. In the Satipatthana Sutta, the Buddha teaches that when walking, a practitioner knows, I am walking. Some Buddhists practice walking as a meditation of its own, attention resting in the feet. So travel time can be practice time, though not every trip in the same way: a driver's practice is full attention on the road. But a walk, a train, a bus, a passenger seat can be a stretch of quiet between the two halves of a day. This week ran through work's corners: envy, a difficult boss, mistakes, a craft, a beginning and an ending. The commute is the road that connects them.
screen: `SAINTE-TERRER: A HOLY-LANDER.` · `THY GOING OUT AND COMING IN.` · `A PRAYER FOR THE ROAD.` · `WHEN WALKING, KNOW IT.` · then, large: `THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Picture the trip you make most often, and imagine making it once with the phone left in a pocket. Let three things from the route come to mind, a tree, a corner, a face; if you drive, picture the road itself, held in full attention. If you pray, you can bring the going out and the coming in to God in your own tradition's words.
The commute. The going out and the coming in, which can be practice time instead of time to be killed. Today's word.
Your line: the road. A trip can be a small pilgrimage. That's the week, and day nine hundred twenty-four.

chat.says: My bus ride feels like wasted time. Can it be anything more?
options: It can be practice time: some traditions bless the road, and walking can be meditation.
Not really; spiritual practice only happens in a quiet room, never on a bus.
Only if you read scripture the whole way; otherwise the time is lost.

notes: Thoreau's Walking paraphrased: 'met with but one or two persons... who had a genius, so to speak, for sauntering' (softened to 'hardly anyone') and his derivation of saunter from Sainte-Terrer. The lesson flags that a dictionary may not agree; confirm that framing is fair.

Tefilat HaDerech: described as said when setting out on a journey, asking to arrive and return in peace; source given as Berakhot 29b–30a from memory. A Judaism Keeper should confirm the source, and whether to note that it is customarily said for journeys beyond a city's limits rather than a daily commute.
Satipatthana Sutta paraphrased ('when walking, he knows I am walking'); a Buddhist Keeper should confirm.
